notes: Slot 2 = PPP (Jawara, Prime Minister; republic referendum pending in 1970). Coalition slot 1 holds the United Party, which was actually the main opposition. The Queen was still head of state on 1 Jan 1970, so slot 23 = House of Windsor. The Gambia had no army; slot 22 = Gambia Field Force. English-language country: native_full/language null.

0.name: The Crown Colony Old Guard
0.text:
The Crown Colony Old Guard are the senior civil servants, British expatriate officers and Aku families of Bathurst who ran the colony before independence in 1965 and still fill many key posts. They regard the protectorate politicians of the People's Progressive Party with open condescension.

They favour firm administrative rule, the retention of the Queen as head of state, close dependence on Britain for aid and advisers, and little patience for mass politics. Their influence rests on control of the administration, the courts and the Field Force officer corps, and on the goodwill of the British High Commission.

1.name: United Party
1.text:
The United Party was founded in 1951 by Pierre Sarr N'Jie, a Bathurst barrister who served as Chief Minister in 1961-62 before losing power to the People's Progressive Party. It is now the main opposition, with its heartland in the capital and among Wolof and Aku voters.

The UP speaks for the urban establishment of the old colony: it is conservative, pro-British and opposed to the republican constitution that the government will put to a referendum in 1970. It accuses the PPP of favouring the protectorate and relies on N'Jie's personal following, Bathurst merchants and the colony's notables.

2.name: People's Progressive Party
2.text:
The People's Progressive Party, founded in 1959 as the Protectorate People's Party, has governed the Gambia since 1962 under Prime Minister Sir Dawda Jawara, a veterinary surgeon from the Mandinka heartland. It led the country to independence in 1965 and is now preparing a second referendum to make the Gambia a republic with an executive president.

The PPP is pragmatic and liberal, upholding multi-party democracy, a free press and a market economy based on groundnut exports. Pro-Western and friendly to both Britain and Senegal, it draws on rural Mandinka voters, the provincial chiefs and a growing educated class, and its majority in Parliament is secure.

3.name: Gambia Workers' Union
3.text:
The Gambia Workers' Union was founded in 1958 by M. E. Jallow and made its name with the general strike of 1961 that won higher wages for Bathurst workers. It organizes dockers, transport and public works labourers and remains the most combative force outside the parties.

The union demands fair wages, the Gambianization of jobs and protection from employer and government pressure, combining labour militancy with social democratic reformism. Its leaders have clashed repeatedly with the PPP government, and its leverage lies in its ability to shut down the port and the capital of a country that lives off a single export.

4.name: The Bathurst Reading Circle
4.text:
The Bathurst Reading Circle is a handful of young civil servants, teachers and returning students who read Marx and Lenin and pass around Soviet and Ghanaian literature brought in from Dakar and London. Some studied in Eastern Europe on scholarships from the socialist bloc.

They argue that the Gambia's independence is hollow as long as British and French trading firms control the groundnut economy, and call for nationalization, land reform and alignment with the Soviet camp. With no party, press or union of their own, their influence is limited to discussion groups and contacts inside the Workers' Union.

5.name: The Black Power Youth
5.text:
The Black Power Youth are school-leavers, unemployed young men and students in Bathurst and the Kombos who have absorbed the slogans of Black Power, Fanon and the Cuban revolution through radio, records and magazines. They gather in tea circles and football clubs rather than parties.

They denounce the PPP as a party of chiefs and elders, attack the privileges of expatriates and Lebanese traders, and dream of a revolutionary Pan-African Gambia. Disorganized and leaderless, they have no electoral weight, but in a country with few jobs for the young their anger could quickly fuel street protest.

6.name: The Kaabu Revivalists
6.text:
The Kaabu Revivalists are elders, griots and rural notables in the upriver provinces who idealize the old Mandinka kingdom of Kaabu and the warrior aristocracy that ruled the Gambia valley before colonial conquest. They see both British rule and modern party politics as alien impositions.

They want customary law, chiefly authority and Islamic morality to prevail over Western schooling, lawyers and the urban elite of Bathurst. Hostile to Western influence and wary of Senegal, they have no organization, but the griots' songs and the loyalty of villages to their lineages give them real sway in the countryside.

7.name: The Nkrumahists
7.text:
The Nkrumahists are former students and young politicians who admired Kwame Nkrumah's Ghana and Sékou Touré's Guinea and believe the Gambia needs a single revolutionary party to break with its colonial past. Nkrumah's overthrow in 1966 shook them, but Touré's Conakry still inspires them.

They would replace the Westminster system with a one-party state, a strong leader, a party militia and close ties with the socialist and radical non-aligned states. Few in number and without a vehicle of their own, they work inside youth and student associations and on the margins of the PPP.

8.name: The Lebanese of Bathurst
8.text:
Bathurst's Lebanese community, largely Shia from southern Lebanon, runs much of the retail trade and many of the groundnut buying stations along the river. Linked by marriage and business to their kin in Dakar, many follow the guidance of Imam Musa al-Sadr and his new Supreme Islamic Shia Council in Lebanon.

The community favours a moderate, socially engaged Shia Islam focused on schools, charity and mutual aid, and keeps out of Gambian party politics. Its leverage lies in its credit, shops and trading networks, which make officials and politicians alike reluctant to cross it.

9.name: The Najaf Circle
9.text:
A few young Lebanese Shia traders in Bathurst, some of whom studied religion in Najaf, follow the teachings of the exiled Iranian cleric Ruhollah Khomeini, who argues that Islamic jurists must govern the state. They exchange books and recorded sermons with like-minded friends in Dakar and Freetown.

The circle rejects both Western liberalism and Soviet communism and hopes for revolutionary clerical rule in the Muslim world. It has no ambitions in the Gambia itself, but its members' ties along the West African trading diaspora make it a potential channel for militant Shia ideas.

10.name: Imam Ratib of Bathurst
10.text:
The Imam Ratib of Bathurst leads the prayers of the capital's central mosque and holds the most senior religious office in the Gambia, passed down within established Muslim families of the town. Around him gather the scholars, mosque committees and Koranic teachers who shape religious life in the capital.

The imamate preaches an orthodox Maliki Sunni Islam that respects the state, endorses the government of the day and opposes both secular radicalism and religious agitation. Its leverage lies in its moral authority over Bathurst's Muslims and its role in national ceremonies, which governments court in return for recognition and support.

11.name: The Al-Azhar Returnees
11.text:
The Al-Azhar returnees are young Gambians who studied Arabic and Islamic law in Cairo, Saudi Arabia and the Maghreb and came home to find no place for their learning in an English-speaking state. A few have been touched by the revolutionary pan-Islamism of Hizb ut-Tahrir and similar movements.

They reject the secular constitution, the authority of the Sufi marabouts and the British legacy, and call for the unity of the Muslim world under a caliphate ruled by sharia. Isolated and few, they preach in family compounds and Koranic schools, drawing on the frustration of the Arabic-educated.

12.name: The Muslim Congress Faithful
12.text:
The Muslim Congress Faithful are Bathurst notables and teachers who remain loyal to the programme of the Gambia Muslim Congress, founded in 1952 by Ibrahima Garba-Jahumpa to give Muslims a political voice against the Christian-educated elite. The party has long since dissolved through mergers, and Garba-Jahumpa now sits in Jawara's cabinet.

The group wants Islamic values in education, family law and public life, Arabic schools alongside English ones and solidarity with the wider Muslim world, pursued through elections. Inspired by reformist movements in Egypt and Senegal, it relies on mosque associations and Muslim traders in the capital.

13.name: The Secretariat
13.text:
The Secretariat is the Gambian civil service at the heart of government in Bathurst: permanent secretaries, finance officials and planners who are steadily replacing British expatriates. Small, close-knit and educated in Britain or Sierra Leone, they run a state that depends almost entirely on groundnut revenue and foreign aid.

They believe in careful administration, balanced budgets and development by plan rather than by politics, and are wary of both party patronage and radical schemes. Neutral in outlook, they deal pragmatically with Britain, Senegal and international donors, and their power lies in drafting every budget and policy the ministers sign.

14.name: The Seyfolu
14.text:
The seyfolu are the district chiefs of the former Protectorate, appointed under British indirect rule and still the government's agents in the countryside. They collect taxes, judge customary cases in district tribunals and sit in the Chiefs' Conference, with several chiefs represented in Parliament.

Conservative and deeply attached to Islam and custom, they back the government of the day in exchange for respect for their authority and salaries. Most have rallied to Jawara's PPP, but their loyalty is conditional, and their control over rural voters, land allocation and local justice makes them indispensable to any ruler.

15.name: The Groundnut Houses
15.text:
The Groundnut Houses are the European trading firms, the United Africa Company, CFAO, Maurel et Prom and their partners, that have dominated the buying, shipping and import trade of the Gambia for generations. Though a state marketing board now buys the crop, they still control wholesale trade, credit and shipping.

They favour low duties, free remittance of profits and a government that keeps the river trade open and orderly. Their influence comes from the Chamber of Commerce, their banks and their place in Britain's aid and trade relations, and few politicians dare to cross them.

16.name: The Albert Market Traders
16.text:
The Albert Market traders are the Wolof, Mandinka and Serahuli merchants who run the stalls of Bathurst's central market and the trade networks reaching deep into Senegal. Much of their business is cross-border re-export, which thrives on the gap between Gambian and Senegalese tariffs.

They want low taxes, minimal regulation and an open border, and oppose any customs union or merger with Senegal that would end the Gambia's role as a free-trade entrepôt. Their leverage lies in their money, their control of everyday supply in the capital and their links to politicians of every party.

17.name: The Abuko Conservationists
17.text:
The Abuko Conservationists are a small group around Eddie Brewer, the British forester who in 1968 persuaded the government to protect the Abuko water catchment as the Gambia's first nature reserve. Volunteers, foresters and expatriate naturalists help him care for its monkeys, crocodiles and rescued animals.

They warn that rapid clearing for groundnuts, firewood cutting and hunting are stripping the Gambia of its forests and wildlife, and press for more reserves and modern wildlife laws. They have no political base, but Brewer's reputation and his contacts with international conservation bodies give them a hearing in government.

18.name: The Senegambia Unionists
18.text:
The Senegambia Unionists are politicians, teachers and civil servants who believe that the Gambia, a narrow enclave inside Senegal, can only prosper in union with its neighbour. They welcome the 1967 treaty of association and its inter-ministerial committee, and admire Senghor's African socialism.

They call for a Senegambian federation with common planning, cooperatives and a shared market, with the state guiding development beyond the groundnut economy. Non-aligned in outlook, they look to Dakar rather than London, but the fear of Senegalese dominance among most Gambians limits their appeal beyond a few educated circles.

19.name: The Red Book Circle
19.text:
The Red Book Circle is a scattering of Gambian students and young teachers who discovered Mao Zedong's writings through Chinese literature distributed in Conakry and through Maoist student groups in Europe. They consider Moscow-oriented Marxists timid revisionists.

They preach peasant revolution against the chiefs, the trading houses and the PPP, admiring China's self-reliance and its support for African liberation movements. With no organization beyond study groups and contacts abroad, they remain marginal, but their message finds an echo among frustrated and jobless youth.

20.name: The River Nationalists
20.text:
The River Nationalists are Bathurst politicians, traders and journalists who fiercely defend Gambian sovereignty against any absorption by Senegal. Many come from the circles of the United Party and the Bathurst press, which accuse the government of preparing to sell the country to Dakar.

They mix populist attacks on politicians and foreigners with pride in the Gambia's English-speaking identity, demanding protection for local traders and jobs for Gambians first. Without a party of their own, their leverage lies in newspapers, market crowds and the deep fear of Senegalese domination that runs through the capital.

21.name: The Iron Hand Club
21.text:
The Iron Hand Club is a loose group of disaffected clerks, ex-servicemen and Field Force men in Bathurst who admire the military strongmen taking power across Africa, from Mobutu's Congo to Eyadéma's Togo. They meet in bars and barracks rather than any party office.

They despise parliamentary talk, ethnic bargaining and the influence of foreigners, and dream of a disciplined nation ruled by a single strong hand that would purge politicians and expel aliens. Tiny and without a recognized leader, they remain a fringe, but their contacts inside the Field Force make them hard to ignore.

22.name: Gambia Field Force
22.text:
The Gambia Field Force is the country's only armed formation, a paramilitary wing of the police created after the colonial Gambia Company was disbanded in 1958. A few hundred men strong and trained by British officers, it guards the capital, the border and key installations.

The Gambia has no army, and the Field Force is firmly subordinate to the government and the Commissioner of Police. Its officers are loyal to the constitution and to Britain's military advisers, but as the only organized armed force in the country it would be the decisive actor if civilian politics ever broke down.

23.name: House of Windsor
23.text:
Queen Elizabeth II of the House of Windsor is still Queen of the Gambia, represented in Bathurst by the Governor-General, Sir Farimang Mamadi Singateh. A 1965 referendum to make the country a republic narrowly failed, and the government is preparing a second vote for 1970.

The monarchy stands for continuity, the Westminster constitution and the Commonwealth link to Britain. Its supporters are found among the Bathurst establishment, the opposition United Party and older Gambians who served the Crown, and they see the Crown as a guarantee against one-party rule.
